summary:
Cusco stands under the national legal framework of Peru. Trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people was removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. No department-level trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for Cusco could be located; every binding rule described here is national in scope and applies in Cusco as elsewhere in Peru.

On 2 April 2025 the Peruvian congressional Plenary approved, exempting it from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their "biological sex", subject only to narrow listed exceptions. The IDEHPUCP legal analysis of Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte holds that this breaches the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests, they argue, on a stigmatising stereotype that presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting indicates that trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

An earlier stage of the same restriction was approved on 20 February 2025, when the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously cleared a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia. That text barred trans people from public restrooms not corresponding to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or when accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banned "ambiguous" bathroom signage. The legislative push followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labelling at Jorge Chávez international airport. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that access would depend on security staff's personal judgement, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The same package of legislation bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity" and carries vague child-protection provisions, including an article 4 prohibition on media and advertising content that enables censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational material. The minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection operates as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. A consumer-protection body, INDECOPI, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the restroom policy, and on television the Willax presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people was stripped from Peru's Penal Code in 2017, when Congress voted to remove it from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The result left Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and, by the account of those recording it, substantially under-counted. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020 to 2023. Trans women were more than half the homicide victims at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 formal complaints logged in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 abduction of the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano by a gang in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, as part of an extortion scheme.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the first torture-by-discrimination case decided by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the restroom provision to discriminate openly against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, following an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom restriction rests on a claimed child-protection rationale that independent bodies reject on the evidence. IDEHPUCP notes that UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors, and Gianna Camacho found no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms, which undercuts the harm the measure purports to prevent.

The removal of LGBT hate-crime coverage in 2017 placed Peru alongside only Paraguay and Guyana in lacking such coverage in South America, leaving trans victims of violence dependent on ordinary offences rather than aggravated hate-crime provisions. That matters for sentence length and for the classification of motive in cases like the Rubí Torres Silvano killing.

Under-recording is a standing caveat on all Peruvian violence figures. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI counts are a registry rather than a full crime statistic, and Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender who co-authored the 2024 report, has stressed that the recorded figures represent only a sub-registry.

The regional human-rights framework runs against the domestic one. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy, and the Inter-American Court's judgment in the Azul Rojas Marín case established regional precedent on torture by discrimination, decided through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The restriction's effects extend beyond state premises. A consumer-protection body's dismissal of a complaint against a private gym, together with televised harassment of a parliamentarian by a presenter, indicates enforcement and social reach into commercial and media settings rather than confined to public buildings.

Speech constraints carry heavy penalties: the obscenity minimum rose from three to four years, and the article 4 ban on media and advertising content gives the April 2025 law reach over identity-related, artistic and educational material, which Human Rights Watch characterises as repression and scapegoating of trans people under a child-protection banner.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cusco are subject to the same national rules as the rest of Peru. There is no department-level trans statute or municipal ordinance governing restroom access, identity documents, healthcare or hate-crime protection; the operative provisions are the April 2025 national law and the earlier congressional bills that preceded it.

The June 2024 revision of official health guidance, which removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity, applies to healthcare settings across the country and is presented as a step toward dignity for trans patients seeking care.

The July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court striking down an anti-equality decree followed an activist legal challenge, indicating that litigation remains an available route for residents challenging discriminatory measures.

Complaints by trans residents about discrimination in commercial premises have a poor record before the national consumer-protection body, which dismissed the complaint against the gym that applied the restroom policy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cusco-specific evidence was located on how the restroom provision is applied in practice in the department: which public buildings it covers, whether security checks or identity-document requests occur locally, and whether any local authority or institution has issued implementing instructions. Enforcement in Cusco is unresolved on the sources available.

The status of bills 6506 and 8457 after the April 2025 law's approval is not fully traced in these sources; the February 2025 committee stage and the 2 April 2025 plenary approval are recorded separately, and the relationship between the two texts is not set out beyond their shared subject matter.

Identity-document and gender-marker rules for trans Peruvians, including whether legal gender recognition is available and on what conditions, are not covered by any source here. The same applies to entry and visa screening that could disclose a trans applicant's status, and to access to gender-affirming healthcare in Cusco beyond the removal of pathologising terminology from national guidance.

The number of killings and rights-violation cases derives from an observatory's registry rather than official crime statistics, and the co-author's own position is that the figures are a sub-registry. National totals for Cusco specifically are not broken out.
